main.title: Dune 2000
main.subtitle: Returning to Arrakis
main.summary: Dune 2000 reached North American Windows players on September 4, 1998.

cards.heading: Dune II remade for a later RTS audience
cards.text: Dune 2000 reached North American Windows players on September 4, 1998. Westwood and Intelligent Games rebuilt Dune II with updated controls, multiplayer, higher-resolution graphics and filmed sequences. Spice harvesting, base construction and rivalry between the Houses remained central, now presented through conventions familiar from Command & Conquer and other late-1990s strategy games.

cards.heading: Updated controls and presentation
cards.text: The remake revisited a design that had helped establish real-time strategy. By 1998, interface and pacing had changed as the genre developed. Westwood brought those later practices back to Dune II's structure, giving players more modern ways to direct units and manage their bases while retaining the setting and its competing Houses.

cards.heading: Keeping the spice moving
cards.text: Spice finances buildings and military units. Harvesters must travel from the base into the desert and return with their cargo, exposing them to enemies and sandworms. Protecting that route is part of maintaining production. A force that loses its harvesters can struggle to replace units or expand, connecting control of the desert to the progress of a campaign.

cards.heading: Orders delivered on film
cards.text: Live-action sequences give faces to the factions and their mission briefings. Actors address the commander directly, presenting the next objective before play returns to the map. The filmed performances help distinguish campaigns built around many of the same resource and construction systems. They also continue the multimedia presentation Westwood had used in Command & Conquer.

main.title: Spyro the Dragon
main.summary: Spyro the Dragon is a 1998 platform game originally developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: A young dragon explores the Homeworlds
cards.text: Spyro the Dragon is a 1998 platform game originally developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. The first game in the Spyro series stars the title character, a young purple dragon named Spyro, and his dragonfly friend, Sparx, who must journey across the Dragon Kingdom to defeat Gnasty Gnorc, who has overtaken the five dragon Homeworlds by trapping the other dragons in crystal and turning their hoard of gems into an army of minions. Spyro the Dragon is an open-ended 3D platformer, featuring large, sprawling levels in which the player must locate collectable items, among which are gemstones, crystallized dragons, and stolen dragon eggs. Spyro's abilities as a dragon include fire breath, a head-on charging attack, and a mid-air glide, which he can use to scale large distances, all of which must be used strategically to find items and defeat enemies.

cards.heading: A dragon built for open landscapes
cards.text: Insomniac began developing Spyro the Dragon following the release of their debut title, Disruptor, which had sold poorly but was praised by critics and impressed Universal Interactive enough for them to encourage the studio to make another game. After artist Craig Stitt suggested a game about a dragon, the team initially drew inspiration from the film Dragonheart, intending the project to be a mature title with a dark, realistic tone. Direction was eventually shifted towards a whimsical and light-hearted tone to appeal to a wider audience. The game was one of the first on the PlayStation to utilize shifting levels of detail among rendered objects, thanks to a panoramic engine developed by Alex Hastings, which allowed the game's open-ended nature to be fully realized. Stewart Copeland, the former drummer for the Police, composed the game's music, and the titular character was voiced by Carlos Alazraqui, with additional voices being provided by Clancy Brown, Michael Gough, and Jamie Alcroft.

cards.heading: Holiday success and a new platforming mascot
cards.text: Spyro helped Sony reach younger players with a colourful platforming character alongside Crash Bandicoot. Sales grew during the 1998 holiday season and eventually approached five million copies. Reviewers praised the graphics, movement and music, with the long view across its landscapes attracting particular attention; some found the challenge too gentle. Insomniac followed it with Ripto's Rage! in 1999 and Year of the Dragon in 2000. All three returned in the 2018 Spyro Reignited Trilogy, preserving the original PlayStation run as a connected set of adventures.

main.title: Pokémon Yellow
main.subtitle: A Companion Walks Outside the Ball
main.summary: On September 12, 1998, Nintendo released Pocket Monsters Pikachu in Japan, known outside the country as Pokémon Yellow.

cards.heading: Pikachu follows the player
cards.text: Nintendo released Pocket Monsters Pikachu in Japan on September 12, 1998, later known internationally as Pokémon Yellow. It revisits the Kanto adventure of Red and Green with additional events and references to the animated series. Pikachu follows the protagonist on screen, expresses its mood when spoken to and uses the familiar television voice. Trading remains compatible with Red, Green and Blue.

cards.heading: A travelling companion with moods
cards.text: Pikachu walks behind the player through towns and routes. Turning to speak to it reveals expressions associated with its mood, making the creature a visible travelling companion. These recurring reactions give players another way to observe their starter beyond its statistics and performance in battle.

cards.heading: A familiar voice on Game Boy
cards.text: Pikachu's cry uses the voice from the animated series, as Nintendo's Virtual Console description later emphasised. Among the first generation's otherwise synthetic creature sounds, the recorded voice is particularly recognisable. Hearing it when interacting with Pikachu directly connects the companion on the Game Boy to the character familiar from television.

cards.heading: The animated series reaches Kanto
cards.text: The anime began in Japan in 1997, and Mewtwo Strikes Back reached cinemas in July 1998. Nintendo also presented Pocket Monsters Pikachu in connection with this first film. The game drew familiar elements from the expanding phenomenon back into Kanto, while retaining the exploration and battles of the original role-playing adventure.

cards.heading: A revised version of a familiar journey
cards.text: Most of Red and Green's story and geography remain in place. Returning players can recognise towns, routes and Gyms while noticing altered events and references to the anime. Pikachu's presence behind the protagonist provides a visible difference throughout that familiar journey. Selected changes give the new version its identity within the same setting.

cards.heading: Trading with the earlier cartridges
cards.text: Yellow retains Game Link Cable trading with Red, Green and Blue. Owners can join the existing community of first-generation players to exchange creatures rather than being confined to others with Yellow. The shared system continues to depend on two Game Boys connected physically, keeping face-to-face exchange central as the franchise expands into television, cards and merchandise.

cards.heading: Following Pokémon in later adventures
cards.text: Nintendo's later discussions of HeartGold and SoulSilver recalled Yellow's following Pikachu as an example of added value within a revised adventure. Later games returned to the idea with more creatures and different hardware. The visible companion first tried here became a recurring way of bringing a player's Pokémon collection into the space being explored.

main.title: Dragon Warrior Monsters
main.summary: Dragon Quest Monsters, released in North America as Dragon Warrior Monsters, is the first video game in the Dragon Quest Monsters series.

cards.text: Dragon Quest Monsters, released in North America as Dragon Warrior Monsters, is the first video game in the Dragon Quest Monsters series. It was released in Japan by Enix on September 25, 1998, and co-published by Eidos Interactive in Europe and North America in 2000. It was the first Dragon Quest game to be released in Europe. The game cartridge is compatible with both the black-and-white Game Boy and the Game Boy Color; a second printing of the game was made after the Game Boy Color itself was released. The game was remade for the PlayStation in a compilation Dragon Quest Monsters 1+2 Hoshi Furi no Yūsha to Bokujō no Nakamatachi. A mobile phone incarnation titled Dragon Quest Monsters i was released in Japan on January 28, 2002.

The game features the characters Terry and Milly from Dragon Quest VI when they were children, before the events in Dragon Quest VI. Dragon Warrior Monsters is often compared to the Pokémon series due to their similar gameplay. Critics set the games apart by noting the in-depth breeding system seen in this game.

In May 2012, a remake of the game for the Nintendo 3DS, titled Dragon Quest Monsters: Terry no Wonderland 3D, was released only in Japan. A smartphone release followed in November 2018, and the game reached Nintendo Switch in September 2019.

main.title: MediEvil
main.subtitle: A second chance for a false hero
main.summary: MediEvil is Sony's PlayStation action-adventure, first released in Europe on 9 October 1998. Sir Daniel Fortesque is remembered as Gallowmere's great champion, although he actually fell to the first arrow of the battle that made his reputation. When the sorcerer Zarok returns a century later, his magic accidentally revives Dan along with the dead. The skeletal knight now has a chance to earn the legend attributed to him. His journey mixes Halloween creatures and comic misfortune, making the unlikely hero's awkward appearance part of the adventure rather than an obstacle to it.

cards.heading: A second chance for a false hero
cards.text: MediEvil is Sony's PlayStation action-adventure, first released in Europe on 9 October 1998. Sir Daniel Fortesque is remembered as Gallowmere's great champion, although he actually fell to the first arrow of the battle that made his reputation. When the sorcerer Zarok returns a century later, his magic accidentally revives Dan along with the dead. The skeletal knight now has a chance to earn the legend attributed to him. His journey mixes Halloween creatures and comic misfortune, making the unlikely hero's awkward appearance part of the adventure rather than an obstacle to it.

cards.heading: The arm is always available
cards.text: Dan fights with swords, clubs, crossbows and other weapons, some of which can be charged for stronger attacks. A club can also open a route, giving equipment a role in exploration. With nothing else available, Dan can detach his own arm and use it to strike or throw. Shields offer protection but wear out, so defence consumes another limited resource. Gargoyle heads provide advice or sell ammunition and services. The collection of tools turns each level into a question of what to spend, what to preserve and which object might reveal a passage.

cards.heading: Earning a place in the hall
cards.text: Defeating enough suitable enemies fills a level's Chalice of Souls. Leaving with it opens a visit to the Hall of Heroes, where its residents can reward Dan with new weapons. The optional collection therefore reinforces his attempt to become a real hero, while Life Bottles increase how much punishment he can survive. Chris Sorrell and Jason Wilson developed the game's character and setting, accompanied by Andrew Barnabas and Paul Arnold's score. MediEvil 2 followed in 2000; later reinterpretations returned to this first adventure on PSP and PlayStation 4.

main.title: Body Harvest
main.subtitle: DMA Design · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Body Harvest is DMA Design's Nintendo 64 action adventure about Adam Drake, a soldier travelling through time to stop aliens from harvesting Earth's population. The campaign moves between periods and regions, including Greece, Java and the United States, with people to protect and a threat developing across each area. Adam explores on foot and commandeers vehicles, giving the player several ways to approach the surrounding terrain. The next useful machine can change both the speed of travel and the means available for confronting an attacking creature.

cards.heading: Return to the invasion before it succeeds
cards.text: Body Harvest is DMA Design's Nintendo 64 action adventure about Adam Drake, a soldier travelling through time to stop aliens from harvesting Earth's population. The campaign moves between periods and regions, including Greece, Java and the United States, with people to protect and a threat developing across each area. Adam explores on foot and commandeers vehicles, giving the player several ways to approach the surrounding terrain. The next useful machine can change both the speed of travel and the means available for confronting an attacking creature.

cards.heading: The nearest vehicle becomes another tool
cards.text: Cars, boats and aircraft extend the expedition beyond the soldier's own movement. Entering one changes which route can be taken and how an encounter can be handled, while leaving it returns attention to local exploration and the people nearby. The player has to respond to the invasion as it develops rather than only move toward a fixed exit. A distant attack can make another destination urgent, connecting navigation through the region to the survival of its inhabitants.

cards.heading: A world larger than the immediate fight
cards.text: Originally planned around the Nintendo 64's launch, the project underwent substantial changes and eventually reached release in 1998 through different publishers. DMA Design was also developing Grand Theft Auto during this period. Body Harvest's interest in moving between a person and accessible vehicles gave its large regions a distinctive structure. The result can be demanding and uneven, but its central ambition is clear: a landscape should contain several practical ways to travel and act, with the player choosing which one the current emergency needs.

main.title: Tetris DX
main.subtitle: Nintendo · Game Boy Color
main.summary: Tetris DX is Nintendo's Game Boy Color version of the falling-block puzzle, released with the new handheld generation in Japan in 1998. Tetrominoes still have to be rotated and arranged into complete horizontal lines before the growing stack reaches the top. Colour helps distinguish their shapes, while saved profiles and additional modes give repeated sessions a longer record. The game preserves the immediate clarity of the original portable Tetris, then changes the surrounding goals so that the same arrangement skills can be tested in several different ways.

cards.heading: The familiar well acquires more ways to play
cards.text: Tetris DX is Nintendo's Game Boy Color version of the falling-block puzzle, released with the new handheld generation in Japan in 1998. Tetrominoes still have to be rotated and arranged into complete horizontal lines before the growing stack reaches the top. Colour helps distinguish their shapes, while saved profiles and additional modes give repeated sessions a longer record. The game preserves the immediate clarity of the original portable Tetris, then changes the surrounding goals so that the same arrangement skills can be tested in several different ways.

cards.heading: Forty lines or two minutes
cards.text: Marathon follows the familiar continuing game, while 40 Lines asks how quickly a fixed target can be reached. Ultra instead gives the player two minutes to create the strongest result. These limits change how the well is managed: a safe long-term structure and a fast short attempt do not always ask for the same placement. Versus play offers computer opponents or another person through the Game Link Cable, turning the puzzle into a direct contest. Each mode gives the next piece a different practical context.

cards.heading: A score that survives the power switch
cards.text: Up to four profiles record names, high scores and performance information, allowing several people to build their own history on the cartridge. The convenience makes another short attempt feel connected to what was achieved before. Nintendo developed the game around preserving Tetris's core rather than adding a complicated replacement for it. The result suits the handheld's daily use: the rule can be understood immediately, while a saved target or a different time limit supplies another reason to return after the screen has been switched off.

main.title: Space Station Silicon Valley
main.subtitle: DMA Design · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Space Station Silicon Valley is DMA Design's Nintendo 64 platform adventure about Evo, a robot reduced to a crawling microchip after a crash. He must occupy the station's robotic animals to survive, solve problems and recover the parts of his body. A creature is therefore both an inhabitant and a possible tool. Its movement and attacks determine what can be done next. The playful menagerie gives the game an immediately unusual question: which of the animals already present would make this particular route possible?

cards.heading: A small chip needs another body
cards.text: Space Station Silicon Valley is DMA Design's Nintendo 64 platform adventure about Evo, a robot reduced to a crawling microchip after a crash. He must occupy the station's robotic animals to survive, solve problems and recover the parts of his body. A creature is therefore both an inhabitant and a possible tool. Its movement and attacks determine what can be done next. The playful menagerie gives the game an immediately unusual question: which of the animals already present would make this particular route possible?

cards.heading: The right animal changes the route
cards.text: Each body has different characteristics, including its ability to survive in the surrounding environment. A large animal may break an obstruction that another cannot, while a different movement allows access to a previously unreachable place. Evo has to leave one body and find another as objectives develop. The environments become collections of related possibilities rather than stages designed around a single permanent hero. Recognising the useful creature can be as important as defeating an enemy, because the next problem may depend on borrowing what that creature can do.

cards.heading: A menagerie with a peculiar sense of humour
cards.text: Dan Danger remains near the damaged spaceship, assigning objectives and commenting on Evo's progress. The animal designs and absurd situations give the station a comic character, supported by Stuart Ross's music. Released in 1998, the game later received adaptations for Game Boy Color and PlayStation, the latter titled Evo's Space Adventures. Its most distinctive quality belongs to the original relationship between the tiny robot and its borrowed bodies. Changing character becomes a practical act performed inside the world, with each new animal briefly redefining the player's capabilities.

main.title: Legend of Legaia
main.subtitle: A world behind the Mist
main.summary: Legend of Legaia is Prokion's PlayStation role-playing game, released in Japan on 29 October 1998 with production by Contrail. Humanity once depended on magical creatures called Seru, but a spreading Mist has turned them violent and broken much of civilisation. Vahn leaves the village of Rim Elm with Meta, a Ra-Seru unaffected by the Mist, seeking to restore the Genesis Trees that can drive it away. Noa and Gala join the journey. The story gives the party a visible reason to enter dangerous territory: each restored tree can make an inhabited place safe again.

cards.heading: A world behind the Mist
cards.text: Legend of Legaia is Prokion's PlayStation role-playing game, released in Japan on 29 October 1998 with production by Contrail. Humanity once depended on magical creatures called Seru, but a spreading Mist has turned them violent and broken much of civilisation. Vahn leaves the village of Rim Elm with Meta, a Ra-Seru unaffected by the Mist, seeking to restore the Genesis Trees that can drive it away. Noa and Gala join the journey. The story gives the party a visible reason to enter dangerous territory: each restored tree can make an inhabited place safe again.

cards.heading: Writing an attack with directions
cards.text: The Tactical Arts System asks the player to build an attack from a sequence of directional commands. Confirming the choice makes the character perform those blows, while particular orders produce stronger Arts. Compatible sequences can overlap, allowing techniques to join into a longer combination. The Spirit command reduces incoming damage and prepares a longer attack on the next turn. That makes waiting an active choice: defend now to create a better opening later. Ordinary encounters become opportunities to learn the body's combinations as well as compare equipment, health and the enemy's remaining strength.

cards.heading: Companions carried on the arm
cards.text: Ra-Seru change the party's attacks and let characters absorb the essence of certain defeated Seru. Those creatures can then be summoned at a magic-point cost, adding another use for encounters already completed. Arts use a separate resource, recovered through attacks, damage or Spirit, so physical combinations and magical assistance ask for different preparation. Michiru Ōshima composed the score for the journey. North American and European releases followed in 1999 and 2000. Legaia 2: Duel Saga later brought a separate cast to PlayStation 2, while the original remained centred on Vahn's struggle against the Mist.

main.title: Fallout 2
main.summary: Fallout 2: A Post Nuclear Role Playing Game is a 1998 role-playing video game developed by Black Isle Studios and published by Interplay Productions.

cards.heading: The Chosen One leaves home
cards.text: Fallout 2: A Post Nuclear Role Playing Game is a 1998 role-playing video game developed by Black Isle Studios and published by Interplay Productions. It is a sequel to Fallout (1997), featuring similar graphics and game mechanics. The game's story takes place in 2241, roughly 80 years after the events of Fallout and 164 years after the atomic war which reduced the vast majority of the world to a nuclear wasteland. The player assumes the role of the Chosen One, the grandchild of the first game's protagonist, and undertakes a quest to save their small village on the West Coast of the United States.

cards.heading: Reception and the later Fallout series
cards.text: Fallout 2 was well received by critics, who praised its gameplay and storyline, and considered it a worthy successor to the original Fallout and one of the greatest games of all time. Its bugs and limited updates to the formula of the first game attracted criticism. In 2008, it was followed by a sequel, Fallout 3, developed by Bethesda Game Studios.
